claim: Esociformes diverged from their sister group Salmoniformes about 110 million years ago.
source: Esociformes is a small order of teleost fishes (Figure 1) that diverged from their sister group Salmoniformes about 110 million years ago (Mya) and diversified from a common ancestor around 90 Mya (Campbell et al., 2013; Campbell and Lopéz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2013 and Campbell and Lopéz, 2014.

claim: Esociformes diversified from a common ancestor around 90 million years ago.
source: Esociformes is a small order of teleost fishes (Figure 1) that diverged from their sister group Salmoniformes about 110 million years ago (Mya) and diversified from a common ancestor around 90 Mya (Campbell et al., 2013; Campbell and Lopéz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2013 and Campbell and Lopéz, 2014.

claim: Esociformes comprises two families: Esocidae (including Esox, Novumbra, and Dallia) and Umbridae (including Umbra).
source: With two families (Esocidae, including Esox, Novumbra, and Dallia, and Umbridae, including Umbra) and 13 well-recognized species (Warren et al., 2020), Esociformes is an ecologically important group of freshwater species from the northern hemisphere (Campbell et al., 2013; Campbell and Lopéz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warren et al., 2020.

claim: Esociformes comprises 13 well-recognized species.
source: With two families (Esocidae, including Esox, Novumbra, and Dallia, and Umbridae, including Umbra) and 13 well-recognized species (Warren et al., 2020), Esociformes is an ecologically important group of freshwater species from the northern hemisphere (Campbell et al., 2013; Campbell and Lopéz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warren et al., 2020.

claim: Esociformes is an ecologically important group of freshwater species from the northern hemisphere.
source: With two families (Esocidae, including Esox, Novumbra, and Dallia, and Umbridae, including Umbra) and 13 well-recognized species (Warren et al., 2020), Esociformes is an ecologically important group of freshwater species from the northern hemisphere (Campbell et al., 2013; Campbell and Lopéz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2013 and Campbell and Lopéz, 2014.

claim: A male-specific duplication of the anti-Müllerian hormone gene (amhby) is the master sex-determining gene in Esociformes.
source: We demonstrated that a male-specific duplication of the anti-Müllerian hormone gene (amhby) is the MSD gene in Esociformes and that this gene is located in a small male-specific insertion on the Y chromosome of northern pike (Esox lucius) (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2019.

claim: The amhby gene is located in a small male-specific insertion on the Y chromosome of northern pike (Esox lucius).
source: We demonstrated that a male-specific duplication of the anti-Müllerian hormone gene (amhby) is the MSD gene in Esociformes and that this gene is located in a small male-specific insertion on the Y chromosome of northern pike (Esox lucius) (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2019.

claim: The northern pike master sex-determining gene amhby originated from a 65 to 90 million-year-old gene duplication event.
source: We discovered that the northern pike (Esox lucius) master sex-determining gene originated from a 65 to 90 million-year-old gene duplication event and that it remained sex linked on undifferentiated sex chromosomes for at least 56 million years in multiple species.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript, including phylogenetic analysis and time-calibrated phylogeny.

claim: The amhby gene remained sex linked on undifferentiated sex chromosomes for at least 56 million years in multiple species.
source: We discovered that the northern pike (Esox lucius) master sex-determining gene originated from a 65 to 90 million-year-old gene duplication event and that it remained sex linked on undifferentiated sex chromosomes for at least 56 million years in multiple species.
evidence: The claim is supported by data on sex linkage across multiple species and phylogenetic timing.

claim: Several independent species- or population-specific sex determination transitions were identified in Esociformes.
source: We identified several independent species- or population-specific sex determination transitions, including a recent loss of a Y chromosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic and population genetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A recent loss of a Y chromosome occurred in some populations of northern pike.
source: We identified several independent species- or population-specific sex determination transitions, including a recent loss of a Y chromosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq and RAD-Seq data showing absence of Y-specific sequences in North American populations.

claim: Occasional sex reversals and genetic bottlenecks provide a non-adaptive explanation for sex determination transitions.
source: We hypothesize that occasional sex reversals and genetic bottlenecks provide a non-adaptive explanation for sex determination transitions.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on inference from population genetic patterns and known phenomena.

claim: Genetic sex determination evolved independently and repeatedly in diverse taxa, including animals, plants, and fungi.
source: Genetic sex determination (GSD) evolved independently and repeatedly in diverse taxa, including animals, plants, and fungi (Tree of Sex Consortium et al., 2014; Beukeboom and Perrin, 2014), but the stability of such systems varies drastically among groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tree of Sex Consortium et al., 2014 and Beukeboom and Perrin, 2014.

claim: The stability of genetic sex determination systems varies drastically among groups.
source: Genetic sex determination (GSD) evolved independently and repeatedly in diverse taxa, including animals, plants, and fungi (Tree of Sex Consortium et al., 2014; Beukeboom and Perrin, 2014), but the stability of such systems varies drastically among groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tree of Sex Consortium et al., 2014 and Beukeboom and Perrin, 2014.

claim: In mammals and birds, conserved male or female heterogametic sex determination systems have been maintained over a long evolutionary time with conserved master sex-determining genes.
source: In mammals and birds, conserved male or female heterogametic sex determination (SD) systems have been maintained over a long evolutionary time with conserved master sex-determining (MSD) genes (Marshall Graves, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marshall Graves, 2008.

claim: Teleost fishes display both genetic and environmental sex determination.
source: In contrast, teleost fishes display both genetic and environmental sex determination (ESD), and a remarkable evolutionary lability driven by rapid turnovers of sex chromosomes and MSD genes (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013 and Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Teleost fishes display remarkable evolutionary lability driven by rapid turnovers of sex chromosomes and master sex-determining genes.
source: In contrast, teleost fishes display both genetic and environmental sex determination (ESD), and a remarkable evolutionary lability driven by rapid turnovers of sex chromosomes and MSD genes (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013 and Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Teleosts are an attractive group in which to study the evolution of sex determination systems.
source: These characteristics make teleosts an attractive group in which to study the evolution of SD systems.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the characteristics of teleosts described in the preceding sentences.

claim: The identity of a variety of master sex-determining genes has been revealed in teleosts in the past two decades thanks to advances in sequencing technologies.
source: In the past two decades, the identity of a variety of MSD genes has been revealed in teleosts thanks to advances in sequencing technologies.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and context.

claim: The birth of master sex-determining genes through allelic diversification or duplication with or without translocation may drive sex chromosome turnover in vertebrates.
source: These findings generated new hypotheses on how the birth of MSD genes through allelic diversification or duplication with or without translocation may drive sex chromosome turnover in vertebrates (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013 and Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Teleost master sex-determining genes provided empirical support for the 'limited option' idea that certain genes known to be implicated in sex differentiation pathways are more likely to be recruited as new master sex-determining genes.
source: These teleost MSD genes also provided empirical support for the 'limited option' idea that states that certain genes known to be implicated in sex differentiation pathways are more likely to be recruited as new MSD genes (Marshall Graves and Peichel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marshall Graves and Peichel, 2010.

claim: The majority of recently discovered master sex-determining genes in teleosts were phylogenetically scattered, making it challenging to infer evolutionary patterns.
source: The majority of these recently discovered MSD genes, however, were phylogenetically scattered, making it challenging to infer evolutionary patterns and conserved themes of sex chromosomes and/or MSD gene turnovers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the distribution of discovered MSD genes.

claim: Comparative studies on sex determination have been accomplished in medakas, poeciliids, tilapiine cichlids, salmonids, and sticklebacks.
source: Although comparative studies have been accomplished in medakas, poeciliids, tilapiine cichlids, salmonids, and sticklebacks (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013), transitions of SD systems in relation to the fate of known MSD genes within closely related species have only been explored in medakas (Myosho et al., 2015) and salmonids (Guiguen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013.

claim: Transitions of sex determination systems in relation to the fate of known master sex-determining genes within closely related species have only been explored in medakas and salmonids.
source: Although comparative studies have been accomplished in medakas, poeciliids, tilapiine cichlids, salmonids, and sticklebacks (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013), transitions of SD systems in relation to the fate of known MSD genes within closely related species have only been explored in medakas (Myosho et al., 2015) and salmonids (Guiguen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Myosho et al., 2015 and Guiguen et al., 2018.

claim: Two amh genes were found in all surveyed Esox and Novumbra species.
source: We found two amh genes in all surveyed Esox and Novumbra species.
evidence: The claim is supported by homology cloning and whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: Only one amh gene was found in both Dallia pectoralis and Umbra pygmaea in tissue-specific transcriptome databases.
source: In the more basally diverging species, Dallia pectoralis and Umbra pygmaea, we found only one amh gene in both species in tissue-specific transcriptome databases (Pasquier et al., 2016), while two amh transcripts were readily identified in E. lucius (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from transcriptome databases cited as Pasquier et al., 2016.

claim: Two amh transcripts were readily identified in E. lucius.
source: In the more basally diverging species, Dallia pectoralis and Umbra pygmaea, we found only one amh gene in both species in tissue-specific transcriptome databases (Pasquier et al., 2016), while two amh transcripts were readily identified in E. lucius (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2019.

claim: Phylogenetic trees of amh sequences provided a clear and consistent topology with two well-supported gene clusters among the amh sequences from Esocidae.
source: These phylogenies provided a clear and consistent topology with two well-supported gene clusters among the amh sequences from Esocidae (Figure 2A, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 2A and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The first gene cluster contains the autosomal amha of E. lucius and an amh homolog from all other species of Esox, Dallia, and Novumbra.
source: The first gene cluster contains the autosomal amha of E. lucius and an amh homolog from all other species of Esox, Dallia, and Novumbra.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The second gene cluster contains the Y-specific amhby gene of E. lucius, along with the other amh homolog from all species for which two amh sequences were identified.
source: The second gene cluster contains the Y-specific amhby gene of E. lucius, along with the other amh homolog from all species for which we identified two amh sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The general topology of each amh gene cluster was in agreement with the Esociformes species taxonomy.
source: The general topology of each cluster was in agreement with the Esociformes species taxonomy.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: In U. pygmaea, the single amh homolog roots at the base of the amha/amhby clusters.
source: In U. pygmaea, the closest sister species to the Esocidae, we found a single amh homolog, which roots at the base of the amha/amhby clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: The amh duplication happened after the divergence of Esocidae and Umbridae lineages.
source: This result indicates that the amh duplication happened after the divergence of Esocidae (including Esox, Dallia, and Novumbra) and Umbridae (including Umbra) lineages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis showing U. pygmaea's single amh gene roots at the base of the amha/amhby clusters.

claim: Dallia pectoralis experienced a secondary loss of its amhby gene after the amh duplication at the root of the Esocidae lineage.
source: In contrast to other Esocidae that have two amh orthologs, we found only one amh gene in D. pectoralis, which fell in the phylogeny within the amha ortholog cluster, suggesting that this species experienced a secondary loss of its amhby gene after the amh duplication at the root of the Esocidae lineage (Figure 2B and Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and supported by Figure 2B and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The absence of an additional divergent amh gene in D. pectoralis was confirmed by searching sex-specific Pool-Seq reads from 30 males and 30 females.
source: We confirmed the absence of an additional divergent amh gene in D. pectoralis by searching sex-specific Pool-Seq reads from 30 males and 30 females.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq data analysis.

claim: Only one amh homolog was found in an ongoing genome assembly project with long reads for a male D. pectoralis.
source: In addition, only one amh homolog was found in an ongoing genome assembly project with long reads for a male D. pectoralis (Y. Guiguen, personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from an ongoing genome assembly project.

claim: The amhby duplicate arose between 65 and 90 million years ago.
source: Using information from an Esociformes time-calibrated phylogeny (Campbell et al., 2013), we estimated that the amhby duplicate arose between 65 and 90 Mya (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from time-calibrated phylogeny data cited from Campbell et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An association between male phenotype and the presence of amhby was found in most species of Esox and Novumbra.
source: We found an association between male phenotype and the presence of amhby in most species of Esox and Novumbra (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Sex linkage of amhby was significant in European, Asian, and Alaskan populations of E. lucius.
source: This sex linkage was significant in European, Asian, and Alaskan populations of E. lucius, in two North American populations of E. masquinongy (Iowa and Wisconsin), and in all populations surveyed of E. reichertii, E. americanus, E. niger, and N. hubbsi.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Sex linkage of amhby was significant in two North American populations of E. masquinongy (Iowa and Wisconsin).
source: This sex linkage was significant in European, Asian, and Alaskan populations of E. lucius, in two North American populations of E. masquinongy (Iowa and Wisconsin), and in all populations surveyed of E. reichertii, E. americanus, E. niger, and N. hubbsi.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Sex linkage of amhby was significant in all populations surveyed of E. reichertii, E. americanus, E. niger, and N. hubbsi.
source: This sex linkage was significant in European, Asian, and Alaskan populations of E. lucius, in two North American populations of E. masquinongy (Iowa and Wisconsin), and in all populations surveyed of E. reichertii, E. americanus, E. niger, and N. hubbsi.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: amhby is present in all males and absent from all females in E. cisalpinus and E. aquitanicus.
source: We confirmed the presence of amhby in all males and its absence from all females in these two species, but the association was not significant due to low sample size (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The association of amhby with male phenotype was not significant in E. cisalpinus and E. aquitanicus due to low sample size.
source: We confirmed the presence of amhby in all males and its absence from all females in these two species, but the association was not significant due to low sample size (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: amhby likely gained a master sex-determining role shortly after its origin either at the root of Esocidae or before the split of Esox and Novumbra lineages (~56 Mya).
source: Because amhby is associated with male phenotype in most species of Esox and Novumbra, it likely gained an MSD role shortly after its origin either at the root of Esocidae or before the split of Esox and Novumbra lineages (~56 Mya) (Campbell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from sex linkage data and phylogenetic timing cited from Campbell et al., 2013.

claim: Variations in amhby sex association exist across populations of E. lucius and E. masquinongy.
source: Despite this global conservation of the linkage between amhby and male phenotype, however, we found some variations in amhby sex association across populations of E. lucius and E. masquinongy (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: A single region of less than 50 kb containing the highest density of male-specific SNPs in E. masquinongy is located in a region homologous to the proximal end of LG24, where the sex locus of E. lucius is located.
source: Comparison of the sex-specific heterozygosity across the entire genome revealed that a single region of less than 50 kb, containing the highest density of male-specific single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in E. masquinongy, is located in a region homologous to the proximal end of LG24, where the sex locus of E. lucius is located.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq analysis data.

claim: No linkage group other than LG24 showed enrichment for sex-biased chromosome differentiation in E. masquinongy.
source: Besides LG24, no other linkage group showed enrichment for sex-biased chromosome differentiation (Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that the location and the small size of the sex locus are likely conserved between E. lucius and E. masquinongy.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The location and the small size of the sex locus are likely conserved between E. lucius and E. masquinongy.
source: Besides LG24, no other linkage group showed enrichment for sex-biased chromosome differentiation (Appendix 1—figure 2), suggesting that the location and the small size of the sex locus are likely conserved between E. lucius and E. masquinongy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Pool-Seq analysis data showing no sex-biased differentiation outside LG24.

claim: Two RAD-Seq markers showed a significant association with male sex in N. hubbsi.
source: We found two markers showing a significant association with male sex and no female-biased marker (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No female-biased marker was found in N. hubbsi.
source: We found two markers showing a significant association with male sex and no female-biased marker (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: N. hubbsi has a male heterogametic sex determination system (XX/XY).
source: This result supports the male heterogametic SD system (XX/XY) that was suggested by the amhby sex linkage and also indicates that the N. hubbsi sex locus is likely small (41.6 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb across the genome, on average, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from RAD-Seq data showing male-biased markers.

claim: The N. hubbsi sex locus is likely small.
source: This result supports the male heterogametic SD system (XX/XY) that was suggested by the amhby sex linkage and also indicates that the N. hubbsi sex locus is likely small (41.6 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb across the genome, on average, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from RAD-Seq data showing only two male-biased markers.

claim: One RAD-Seq marker showed a significant association with females in D. pectoralis, while no marker showed association with males.
source: In D. pectoralis, we found only three female-biased RAD markers, suggesting that this species also has a small sex locus region (30.8 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) under a female heterogametic SD system (ZZ/ZW) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: D. pectoralis has a small sex locus region under a female heterogametic sex determination system (ZZ/ZW).
source: In D. pectoralis, we found only three female-biased RAD markers, suggesting that this species also has a small sex locus region (30.8 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) under a female heterogametic SD system (ZZ/ZW) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from RAD-Seq data showing female-biased markers.

claim: The ZZ/ZW sex determination system in D. pectoralis was further supported by Pool-Seq analysis revealing 45 times more female-specific k-mers than male-specific k-mers.
source: This ZZ/ZW SD system was further supported by an independent Pool-Seq analysis revealing 45 times more female-specific k-mers (N = 1,081,792) than male-specific k-mers (N = 23,816).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq k-mer analysis data.

claim: The excess of female-specific k-mers in D. pectoralis indicates that females carry genomic regions that are absent from males and thus that females are the heterogametic sex.
source: This excess of female-specific k-mers indicates that females carry genomic regions that are absent from males and thus that females are the heterogametic sex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Pool-Seq k-mer analysis data.

claim: 140 male-biased and no female-biased RAD markers were identified in U. pygmaea.
source: In contrast, 140 male-biased and no female-biased RAD markers were identified in U. pygmaea, supporting that this species has a large sex locus (26.2 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) under a male heterogametic SD system (XX/XY) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: U. pygmaea has a large sex locus under a male heterogametic sex determination system (XX/XY).
source: In contrast, 140 male-biased and no female-biased RAD markers were identified in U. pygmaea, supporting that this species has a large sex locus (26.2 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) under a male heterogametic SD system (XX/XY) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from RAD-Seq data showing many male-biased markers.

claim: amhby was absent from the genome assembly of a male specimen from a Canadian population of northern pike.
source: Although amhby is the MSD gene in European populations of northern pike (Pan et al., 2019), this gene was absent from the genome assembly (GCA_000721915.3) of a male specimen from a Canadian population (GCA_000721915.3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from genome assembly analysis.

claim: amhby showed significant male linkage in all investigated European and Asian populations of E. lucius and in one Alaskan population.
source: We found significant male linkage in all investigated European and Asian populations and in one Alaskan population (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: amhby was absent from both males and females in all North American populations of E. lucius except Alaska.
source: In contrast, amhby was absent from both males and females in all other North American populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Pool-Seq analysis confirmed the presence of a small Y chromosome region (~140 kb) characterized by many male-specific sequences at the proximal end of LG24 in the European population of E. lucius.
source: In the European population, Pool-Seq analysis confirmed, with better resolution, previous results (Pan et al., 2019), showing the presence of a small Y chromosome region (~140 kb) characterized by many male-specific sequences at the proximal end of LG24 (Figure 4 A.1 and 4B.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 4 A.1 and 4B.1.

claim: Virtually no reads from either male or female pools from the Quebec population of E. lucius mapped to the 140 kb Y-specific region.
source: In comparison, virtually no reads from either male or female pools from the Quebec population mapped to this 140 kb Y-specific region (Figure 4 A.2 and 4B.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 4 A.2 and 4B.2.

claim: No differentiation between males and females was observed along the remainder of the genome in the Quebec population of E. lucius with either Pool-Seq or reference-free RAD-Seq.
source: Furthermore, we observed no differentiation between males and females along the remainder of the genome with either Pool-Seq or reference-free RAD-Seq (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq and RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The Quebec population and likely other mainland US populations of E. lucius lack not only amhby, but also the surrounding Y-specific region identified in European populations.
source: Together, these results suggest that the Quebec population and likely other mainland US populations, where the MSD gene amhby was not found, lack not only amhby, but also the surrounding Y-specific region identified in European populations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Pool-Seq and RAD-Seq data showing absence of Y-specific sequences.

claim: The new sex locus of North American populations of E. lucius, if it exists, is too small to be detected by the RAD-Seq and Pool-Seq approaches.
source: Moreover, the new sex locus of these North American populations, if it exists, is too small to be detected by the RAD-Seq and Pool-Seq approaches.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of sex-specific signals in RAD-Seq and Pool-Seq data.

claim: Variation in amhby sex linkage was found among different populations of E. masquinongy.
source: As in E. lucius, we found variation in amhby sex linkage among different populations of E. masquinongy (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Two males and one female of E. masquinongy from Quebec were heterozygous for amhby.
source: In addition, we found that two males and one female of E. masquinongy were heterozygous for amhby in the population from Quebec (Appendix 1—figure 4), a finding that conflicts with the expected hemizygous status of a Y-specific MSD gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The heterozygous status of amhby in some E. masquinongy individuals conflicts with the expected hemizygous status of a Y-specific master sex-determining gene.
source: In addition, we found that two males and one female of E. masquinongy were heterozygous for amhby in the population from Quebec (Appendix 1—figure 4), a finding that conflicts with the expected hemizygous status of a Y-specific MSD gene.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of heterozygous amhby in individuals.

claim: Five RAD markers were significantly associated with male phenotype in the Iowa population of E. masquinongy, while no marker was associated with female phenotype.
source: In the Iowa population, five RAD markers were significantly associated with male phenotype, while no marker was associated with female phenotype (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Iowa population of E. masquinongy has a male heterogametic sex determination system (XX/XY) with a low differentiation between the X and Y chromosomes.
source: This result indicates a male heterogametic SD system (XX/XY) with a low differentiation between the X and Y chromosomes, as observed in northern pike (Pan et al., 2019) and N. hubbsi (this study).
evidence: The claim is inferred from RAD-Seq data showing male-biased markers.

claim: No sex-specific marker was found in the Quebec population of E. masquinongy.
source: In contrast, we did not find a sex-specific marker in the Quebec population (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The lack of sex-specific markers in the Quebec population of E. masquinongy was further supported by the analysis of a publicly available dataset from another Quebec population.
source: This result was further supported by the analysis of a publicly available dataset from another Quebec population (PRJNA512459, Appendix 1—figure 5), suggesting that the sex locus of E. masquinongy from these Quebec populations is too small to be detected with RAD-Seq (38.4 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) or that this population displays a multifactorial GSD or ESD system.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available RAD-Seq data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: The sex locus of E. masquinongy from Quebec populations is too small to be detected with RAD-Seq or this population displays a multifactorial GSD or ESD system.
source: This result was further supported by the analysis of a publicly available dataset from another Quebec population (PRJNA512459, Appendix 1—figure 5), suggesting that the sex locus of E. masquinongy from these Quebec populations is too small to be detected with RAD-Seq (38.4 restriction enzyme cutting sites/Mb on average, Supplementary file 2) or that this population displays a multifactorial GSD or ESD system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of sex-specific markers in RAD-Seq data.

claim: The typical amh gene in teleost fishes comprises seven exons encoding a protein that contains 500–571 amino acids.
source: The typical amh gene in teleost fishes comprises seven exons encoding a protein that contains 500–571 amino acids.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about amh gene structure in teleosts.

claim: The conserved C-terminal TGF-β domain is crucial for canonical Amh function.
source: The conserved C-terminal TGF-β domain is crucial for canonical Amh function (di Clemente et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to di Clemente et al., 2010.

claim: The predicted structures of most of the amha and amhby genes in Esociformes are consistent with the canonical amh structure.
source: The predicted structures of most of the amha and amhby genes in Esociformes are consistent with this canonical structure, and most amha and amhby genes do not show signature of relaxation from purifying selection (Supplementary file 4 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural prediction data presented in Supplementary files 4 and 5.

claim: Most amha and amhby genes in Esociformes do not show signature of relaxation from purifying selection.
source: The predicted structures of most of the amha and amhby genes in Esociformes are consistent with this canonical structure, and most amha and amhby genes do not show signature of relaxation from purifying selection (Supplementary file 4 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by selection analysis data presented in Supplementary files 4 and 5.

claim: In both E. niger and N. hubbsi, the predicted Amhby protein is truncated in its N- or C-terminal part.
source: However, in both E. niger and N. hubbsi, the predicted Amhby protein is truncated in its N- or C-terminal part.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure prediction data.

claim: In E. niger, the truncated amhby gene is flanked by repeated elements and encompasses only three of the seven conserved Amh exons (exons 5, 6, and 7) with a truncated TGF-β domain.
source: In E. niger, this truncated amhby gene is flanked by repeated elements and encompasses only three of the seven conserved Amh exons, that is exons 5, 6, and 7 with a truncated TGF-β domain (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene structure analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: In N. hubbsi, the truncated amhby gene contains the seven conserved Amh exons but with an N-terminal truncation of exon 1 encoding only eight amino acids with no homology to the conserved 50 amino acid sequence of the first Amh exon of other Esocidae.
source: In N. hubbsi, the truncated amhby gene contains the seven conserved Amh exons but with an N-terminal truncation of exon 1 encoding only eight amino acids with no homology to the conserved 50 amino acid sequence of the first Amh exon of other Esocidae (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene structure analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: In some species where amhby is sex linked, the protein sequence is strongly modified in the N- and C-terminal-conserved domains that are needed for proper protein secretion and correct conformation.
source: Together, these results show that in some species where amhby is sex linked, the protein sequence is strongly modified in the N- and C-terminal-conserved domains that are needed for proper protein secretion and correct conformation (di Clemente et al., 2010), leaving questions as to whether these proteins are functional.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure analysis data and citation to di Clemente et al., 2010.

claim: The northern pike master sex-determining gene amhby substantially diverges from its autosomal copy amha, suggesting an ancient origin.
source: The northern pike MSD gene amhby substantially diverges from its autosomal copy amha, suggesting an ancient origin (Pan et al., 2019), unlike other cases of amh duplication in fishes, that appears to be comparatively young (Hattori et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2019, Hattori et al., 2013, and Li et al., 2015.

claim: Other cases of amh duplication in fishes appear to be comparatively young.
source: The northern pike MSD gene amhby substantially diverges from its autosomal copy amha, suggesting an ancient origin (Pan et al., 2019), unlike other cases of amh duplication in fishes, that appears to be comparatively young (Hattori et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hattori et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2015.

claim: The amhby duplicate emerged before the split of Esocidae and Umbridae between 65 and 90 million years ago.
source: Here, we show that the amhby duplicate emerged before the split of Esocidae and Umbridae between 65 and 90 Mya (Campbell et al., 2013) and was subsequently secondarily lost in the Dallia lineage.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citation to Campbell et al., 2013.

claim: amhby was subsequently secondarily lost in the Dallia lineage.
source: Here, we show that the amhby duplicate emerged before the split of Esocidae and Umbridae between 65 and 90 Mya (Campbell et al., 2013) and was subsequently secondarily lost in the Dallia lineage.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data.

claim: amhby presence is significantly associated with male phenotype in most species of Esox and in Novumbra.
source: We also demonstrate that amhby presence is significantly associated with male phenotype in most species of Esox and in Novumbra.
evidence: The claim is supported by sex linkage data presented in Table 1.

claim: amhby likely acquired a master sex-determining function before the diversification of Esocidae at least 56 million years ago.
source: Although we cannot rule out the possibility that amhby was recruited independently as the MSD gene in Esox and Novumbra, our results suggest the more parsimonious hypothesis that amhby likely acquired an MSD function before the diversification of Esocidae at least 56 Mya.
evidence: The claim is inferred from sex linkage data and phylogenetic timing, presented as the more parsimonious hypothesis.

claim: Studies on sex determination systems of cichlid fishes and true frogs suggested that frequent turnovers can keep sex chromosomes undifferentiated.
source: Studies on SD systems of cichlid fishes and true frogs suggested that frequent turnovers can keep sex chromosomes undifferentiated (Gammerdinger et al., 2018; Jeffries et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gammerdinger et al., 2018 and Jeffries et al., 2018.

claim: In cichlid fishes and true frogs, the turnover of sex chromosomes was facilitated by autosomes that host genes involved in sex differentiation pathways that could be readily recruited as new master sex-determining genes.
source: It was proposed that in these organisms, the turnover of sex chromosomes was facilitated by autosomes that host genes involved in sex differentiation pathways that could be readily recruited as new MSD genes, facilitating turnovers of sex chromosomes (Vicoso, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vicoso, 2019.

claim: Alternative evolutionary pathways could involve conserved master sex-determining genes that translocate onto different autosomes, as demonstrated for the salmonid sdY gene.
source: Alternative evolutionary pathways could also involve conserved MSD genes that translocate onto different autosomes, as demonstrated for the salmonid sdY gene (Guiguen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guiguen et al., 2018.

claim: No highly differentiated sex chromosomes were observed in the surveyed population of E. masquinongy and N. hubbsi, or in E. lucius, despite Esocidae having retained the same ancestral XX/XY system for at least 56 million years.
source: Interestingly, this scenario does not seem to be the case with Esocidae. No highly differentiated sex chromosomes were observed in the surveyed population of E. masquinongy and N. hubbsi (this study), or in E. lucius, despite Esocidae having retained the same ancestral XX/XY system (likely controlled by amhby) for at least 56 million years.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data from this study.

claim: Whole-genome analyses in E. masquinongy suggest that its male-specific locus on the Y chromosome is conserved in terms of size and location with that of E. lucius despite 45 million years of divergence.
source: In addition, whole-genome analyses in E. masquinongy suggest that its male-specific locus on the Y chromosome is conserved in terms of size and location with that of E. lucius despite 45 million years of divergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by Pool-Seq analysis data.

claim: Conservation of undifferentiated sex chromosomes over relatively long evolutionary periods is unusual in teleosts, where frequent turnover of sex determination systems is considered the norm.
source: Such conservation is unusual in teleosts, where frequent turnover of SD systems is considered the norm (Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kikuchi and Hamaguchi, 2013 and Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Substantially undifferentiated sex chromosomes have been maintained over relatively long evolutionary periods in some Takifugu fish species.
source: In line with our present results, substantially undifferentiated sex chromosomes have also been maintained over relatively long evolutionary periods in some Takifugu fish species (Kamiya et al., 2012), supporting the idea that theoretical models of sex chromosome evolution cannot be generalized across taxa and that additional, as-yet unknown evolutionary forces can prevent sex chromosome decay.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kamiya et al., 2012.

claim: Theoretical models of sex chromosome evolution cannot be generalized across taxa and additional, as-yet unknown evolutionary forces can prevent sex chromosome decay.
source: In line with our present results, substantially undifferentiated sex chromosomes have also been maintained over relatively long evolutionary periods in some Takifugu fish species (Kamiya et al., 2012), supporting the idea that theoretical models of sex chromosome evolution cannot be generalized across taxa and that additional, as-yet unknown evolutionary forces can prevent sex chromosome decay.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of undifferentiated sex chromosomes maintained over long periods in multiple taxa.

claim: The master sex-determining gene amhby has been subjected to several independent sex determination transitions in the Esocidae lineage.
source: Even though this MSD gene has been maintained for a long evolutionary period, our results revealed that it has been subjected to several independent SD transitions, potentially driven by different mechanisms in the Esocidae lineage.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic and population genetic data.

claim: In D. pectoralis, a transition from the ancestral XX/XY male heterogametic system to a ZZ/ZW female heterogametic system was observed.
source: In D. pectoralis, we observed a transition from the ancestral XX/XY male heterogametic system shared by Esocidae and U. pygmaea to a ZZ/ZW female heterogametic system.
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq and Pool-Seq data.

claim: The transition to female heterogamety in D. pectoralis coincided with the loss of amhby.
source: This transition also coincided with the loss of amhby.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and genomic data.

claim: The shift from male to female heterogamety in D. pectoralis could have been driven by the rise of a new dominant female determinant, leading to the obsolescence and subsequent loss of the ancestral male master sex-determining gene.
source: This shift from male to female heterogamety could have been driven by the rise of a new dominant female determinant, leading to the obsolescence and the subsequent loss of the ancestral male MSD gene, similar to the transition of SD documented among the Oryzias and also in the housefly (Kozielska et al., 2008, Myosho et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative, drawing on analogies to transitions documented in other species cited as Kozielska et al., 2008 and Myosho et al., 2012.

claim: The sex determination transitions in E. lucius and E. masquinongy are probably more recent because these transitions are found within populations of the same species.
source: The other SD transitions that we characterized, those in E. lucius and E. masquinongy, are probably more recent because these transitions are found within populations of the same species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of population-level variation.

claim: In E. masquinongy, population-specific variation in sex determination systems was observed, supporting the conservation of an XX/XY system with amhby as the master sex-determining gene in two US populations belonging to the northern lineage, but not in a Quebec population belonging to the Great Lakes lineage.
source: In E. masquinongy, we observed population-specific variation in SD systems, supporting the conservation of an XX/XY system with amhby as the MSD gene in two US populations belonging to the northern lineage, but not in a Quebec population belonging to the Great Lakes lineage (Turnquist et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq data and citation to Turnquist et al., 2017 for lineage information.

claim: Although amhby is still present in the genome of the Great Lakes lineage of E. masquinongy, it is no longer the master sex-determining gene and a new population-specific sex determination mechanism emerged after the split of the lineages.
source: This result suggests that although amhby is still present in the genome of the Great Lakes lineage, it is no longer the MSD gene and that a new population-specific SD mechanism emerged after the split of the lineages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of sex linkage of amhby in the Great Lakes lineage.

claim: Female heterogamety was previously inferred for the Great Lakes lineage of E. masquinongy based on the presence of males in the offspring of gynogenetic females.
source: Previously, female heterogamety was inferred for the Great Lakes lineage based on the presence of males in the offspring of gynogenetic females (Dabrowski et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dabrowski et al., 2000.

claim: With RAD-Seq, no evidence for female-specific genomic regions was found in the Great Lakes lineage of E. masquinongy.
source: With RAD-Seq, we did not find evidence for female-specific genomic regions in the Great Lakes lineage of E. masquinongy.
evidence: The claim is supported by RAD-Seq analysis data.

claim: amhby is present and completely sex linked in European, Asian, and Alaskan regions of E. lucius.
source: In E. lucius, we found that amhby is present and completely sex linked in European, Asian, and Alaskan regions, but is not present elsewhere in North America (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by sex linkage data presented in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: amhby is not present elsewhere in North America except Alaska in E. lucius.
source: In E. lucius, we found that amhby is present and completely sex linked in European, Asian, and Alaskan regions, but is not present elsewhere in North America (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by sex linkage data presented in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: amhby functions as a master sex-determining gene in Eurasian and Alaskan populations of E. lucius.
source: This finding suggests that amhby functions as an MSD gene in Eurasian and Alaskan populations, but that populations from elsewhere in North America lost amhby together with the entire sex locus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from sex linkage data.

claim: Populations from elsewhere in North America lost amhby together with the entire sex locus.
source: This finding suggests that amhby functions as an MSD gene in Eurasian and Alaskan populations, but that populations from elsewhere in North America lost amhby together with the entire sex locus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Pool-Seq and RAD-Seq data showing absence of Y-specific sequences.

claim: The current geographic distribution of E. lucius results from a post-glacial expansion from three glacial refugia ~0.18 to 0.26 million years ago.
source: The current geographic distribution of E. lucius results from a post-glacial expansion from three glacial refugia ~0.18 to 0.26 Mya.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about E. lucius biogeography.

claim: The North American populations of E. lucius lacking amhby belong to a monophyletic lineage with a circumpolar distribution originating from the same refugia as the other population surveyed that carry amhby.
source: The North American populations lacking amhby belong to a monophyletic lineage with a circumpolar distribution originating from the same refugia as the other population we surveyed that carry amhby (Skog et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Skog et al., 2014.

claim: Fossil records from Alaska support the idea of an 'out of Alaska' North American expansion of E. lucius within the last 100,000 years.
source: Fossil records from Alaska support the idea of an 'out of Alaska' North American expansion of E. lucius within the last 100,000 years (Wooller et al., 2015), suggesting that the Y-specific sequences containing amhby were lost during this dispersal period (Figure 5, Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wooller et al., 2015.

claim: The Y-specific sequences containing amhby were lost during the dispersal period of E. lucius within the last 100,000 years.
source: Fossil records from Alaska support the idea of an 'out of Alaska' North American expansion of E. lucius within the last 100,000 years (Wooller et al., 2015), suggesting that the Y-specific sequences containing amhby were lost during this dispersal period (Figure 5, Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from fossil records and genomic data showing absence of amhby in North American populations.

claim: The loss of the entire sex locus in North American populations of E. lucius in such a short evolutionary time is unlikely to have resulted from the pseudogenization of the amhby gene.
source: The loss of the entire sex locus in such a short evolutionary time is unlikely to have resulted from the pseudogenization of the amhby gene, as is the case for the ancestral MSD gene of the Luzon medaka (Myosho et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of complete loss of Y-specific sequences and comparison to other cases cited as Myosho et al., 2012.

claim: The loss of the Y chromosome in North American populations of E. lucius is probably the result of colonization by a small pool of females and sex-reversed XX males.
source: Rather, it is probably the result of colonization by a small pool of females and sex-reversed XX males.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presented as a hypothesis.

claim: The founder-effect hypothesis for Y chromosome loss in North American E. lucius is supported by the fact that North American populations display a much lower genetic diversity compared to other populations from the same lineage.
source: Such a founder-effect hypothesis is supported by the fact that North American populations of E. lucius display a much lower genetic diversity compared to other populations from the same lineage (Skog et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Skog et al., 2014.

claim: The founder-effect hypothesis for Y chromosome loss in North American E. lucius is supported by the fact that environmental influence on genetic sex determination systems is a well-documented phenomenon in fishes.
source: This hypothesis is also supported by the fact that environmental influence on GSD systems is a well-documented phenomenon in fishes (Baroiller et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014; Sato et al., 2005) and that XX sex reversal induced by environmental factors has been observed occasionally in captive E. lucius (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baroiller et al., 2009, Chen et al., 2014, and Sato et al., 2005.

claim: XX sex reversal induced by environmental factors has been observed occasionally in captive E. lucius.
source: This hypothesis is also supported by the fact that environmental influence on GSD systems is a well-documented phenomenon in fishes (Baroiller et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014; Sato et al., 2005) and that XX sex reversal induced by environmental factors has been observed occasionally in captive E. lucius (Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2019.

claim: If a new sex locus exists in North American populations of E. lucius, it would lack detectable signatures of sequence differentiation, similar to the one-SNP sex locus of some Takifugu species.
source: Our whole-genome analyses failed to identify any sex-associated signals in these North American populations, meaning that if such a new sex locus exists, it would lack detectable signatures of sequence differentiation, similar to the one-SNP sex locus of some Takifugu species (Kamiya et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of sex-associated signals in genomic data and comparison to Takifugu cited as Kamiya et al., 2012.

claim: Environmental sex determination is common among poikilothermic animals including teleosts.
source: Whether ESD, which is common among poikilothermic animals including teleosts (Navara, 2018), could be the SD system in these North American populations or whether these populations already have a new GSD system in place is still unresolved.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Navara, 2018.

claim: The Y chromosome loss in natural populations of E. lucius mirrors the loss of the W chromosome in lab strains of zebrafish after just a few decades of selective breeding.
source: Notably, this Y chromosome loss in natural populations of E. lucius mirrors the loss of the W chromosome in lab strains of zebrafish after just a few decades of selective breeding (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2014.

claim: A few evolutionary models have been formulated to capture the dynamics of sex chromosome turnover.
source: A few evolutionary models have been formulated to capture the dynamics of sex chromosome turnover (Vicoso, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vicoso, 2019.

claim: The replacement of the ancestral sex determination locus by a new one could be driven by drift alone, by positive selection, by sexual antagonistic selection, or by the accumulation of deleterious mutations at the sex locus.
source: The replacement of the ancestral SD locus by a new one could be driven by drift alone, by positive selection (Bull and Charnov, 1977), by sexual antagonistic selection (van Doorn and Kirkpatrick, 2007), or by the accumulation of deleterious mutations at the sex locus (Blaser et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bull and Charnov, 1977, van Doorn and Kirkpatrick, 2007, and Blaser et al., 2013.

claim: In all evolutionary models of sex chromosome turnover, the ancestral sex chromosomes would revert to autosomes only when the new sex determination locus is fixed in the population.
source: In all of these models, the ancestral sex chromosomes would revert to autosomes only when the new SD locus is fixed in the population.
evidence: The claim is based on established theoretical models of sex chromosome evolution.

claim: In North American populations of E. lucius, the ancestral sex chromosome was likely lost due to drift in bottlenecked populations.
source: However, in North American populations of E. lucius, the ancestral sex chromosome was likely lost due to drift in bottlenecked populations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from population genetic data and presented as a hypothesis.

claim: The process of sex chromosome loss in North American E. lucius would not require the simultaneous emergence of a new genetic sex determination system, given the flexibility of sex determination mechanisms in teleosts.
source: Interestingly, this process would not require the simultaneous emergence of a new GSD system, given the flexibility of SD mechanisms in teleosts, where environmental cues generate phenotypic sexes in the absence of a GSD system.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference about teleost sex determination flexibility.

claim: Environmental sex determination is easily invaded by a new genetic system.
source: ESD, which is easily invaded by a new genetic system (Muralidhar and Veller, 2018; van Doorn, 2014), may serve as a transitional state between sex chromosome turnovers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Muralidhar and Veller, 2018 and van Doorn, 2014.

claim: Environmental sex determination may serve as a transitional state between sex chromosome turnovers.
source: ESD, which is easily invaded by a new genetic system (Muralidhar and Veller, 2018; van Doorn, 2014), may serve as a transitional state between sex chromosome turnovers.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presented as a hypothesis.

claim: A truncated amh duplicate acting as a master sex-determining gene is found in the teleost cobalt silverside Hypoatherina tsurugae.
source: A similar example of a truncated amh duplicate acting as an MSD gene is found in the teleost cobalt silverside Hypoatherina tsurugae (Bej et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bej et al., 2017.

claim: Additional cases of truncated duplicated genes functioning as master sex-determining genes have been described in Salmonids, yellow perch (Perca flavescens), and Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus).
source: Additional cases of truncated duplicated genes functioning as MSD genes have been described in Salmonids, yellow perch (Perca flavescens), and Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus), suggesting that the preservation of ancestral domains is not necessary for a duplicated protein to assume a novel role (Feron et al., 2020b; Rafati et al., 2020; Yano et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feron et al., 2020b, Rafati et al., 2020, and Yano et al., 2012.

claim: The preservation of ancestral domains is not necessary for a duplicated protein to assume a novel role.
source: Additional cases of truncated duplicated genes functioning as MSD genes have been described in Salmonids, yellow perch (Perca flavescens), and Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus), suggesting that the preservation of ancestral domains is not necessary for a duplicated protein to assume a novel role (Feron et al., 2020b; Rafati et al., 2020; Yano et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from examples of truncated MSD genes cited as Feron et al., 2020b, Rafati et al., 2020, and Yano et al., 2012.

claim: Domain gains and losses contribute to new protein functions.
source: These cases are all consistent with domain gains and losses contributing to new protein functions (Moore and Bornberg-Bauer, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moore and Bornberg-Bauer, 2012.
